items.title: RAG vs. retriever-free RAG, clearly explained!
items.summary:
RAG vs. retriever-free RAG, clearly explained!

(powered by decision models like Jev)

In a standard RAG setup, documents are split into chunks, converted into embeddings, and stored in a vector index.

When a query arrives, the system embeds it and pulls the top-k chunks with the closest vectors.

A reranker then reorders those candidates against the query, and the best few go to the LLM as context.

The problem is that the similarity search decides what the LLM can ever see.

If the right passage never made the top-k, nothing later in the pipeline can bring it back, not even a strong reranker.

Retriever-free RAG, from a new Cornell and ASAPP paper, keeps the documents and the LLM but replaces similarity search with navigation.

The documents are organized as a document tree, like a table of contents, and a decision model (Jev 1.13) walks down it.

A decision model doesn't generate text. It reads one shared context and returns a probability for every yes/no question about it, in one forward pass per stage.

Here's how a query moves through the tree:

↳ Top documents: the model reads the query beside every candidate document, asks "Is this relevant?" for each, and keeps the best few.
↳ Top passages: it opens only those documents and asks the same question for every passage inside them.
↳ Most relevant? (optional): a single multiple-choice question reorders the top 20 passages (top 5 on Natural Questions).

Dropped documents are never opened, so their passages are never scored.

On Natural Questions (2.68M Wikipedia paragraphs), its top pick contained the answer 65.4% of the time. Embedding search plus an 8B reranker got 48.0%, and GPT-5 reranking got 60.8%.

The gain comes from ranking, not coverage. Embedding search's top 100 holds the answer more often than the navigated shortlist (98.4% vs 94.0%), but navigation is better at putting it first.

Median retrieval takes under 2 seconds per query, but each method was timed in a different setup, so it isn't a controlled speed comparison.

The main limit is that it needs a sensible hierarchy, and a document pruned early is gone for good. It also skips embedding search only at query time, since the Wikipedia tree was built offline using embeddings.

The diagram below depicts the complete flow.

- RAG retrieves by similarity, then reranks.
- Retriever-free RAG navigates a document tree with a decision model.
- The LLM answers from the top passages.

If you're building a RAG system, this is worth benchmarking against your current setup.

Here's the paper: https://t.co/U7cCcIfZV1

If you're new to decision models, I've quoted my full breakdown of how Jev works below.

items.title: GPT-5 just casually did new mathematics.
items.summary:
GPT-5 just casually did new mathematics.

Sebastien Bubeck gave it an open problem from convex optimization, something humans had only partially solved. GPT-5-Pro sat down, reasoned for 17 minutes, and produced a correct proof improving the known bound from 1/L all the way to 1.5/L.

This wasn’t in the paper. It wasn’t online. It wasn’t memorized. It was new math. Verified by Bubeck himself.

Humans later closed the gap at 1.75/L, but GPT-5 independently advanced the frontier.
A machine just contributed original research-level mathematics.

If you’re not completely stunned by this, you’re not paying attention.

We’ve officially entered the era where AI isn’t just learning math, it’s creating it. @sama @OpenAI @kevinweil @gdb @markchen90

items.title: AI and your job: Threat or opportunity?
items.summary:
MOBILE, Ala. (WALA) - Artificial intelligence is becoming a bigger part of everyday life, raising questions about what the technology could mean for workers and their jobs.

Some economists believe AI poses a particular threat to entry-level and repetitive work, including call center, data entry and junior copywriting jobs, according to The Wall Street Journal. Those tasks may be easier to automate. [...] But AI could also create opportunities. A Bloomberg article points to potential job growth in construction and manufacturing as companies build data centers and produce the chips that power the technology. Some higher-skilled office workers could also benefit if AI helps them become more productive. [...] The long-term impact on jobs remains unclear, but workers can take steps to prepare. Exploring AI chatbots, writing assistants and other tools may help people find ways to work more efficiently and develop skills that complement the technology.

items.summary: I understand the appeal. College is busy. Between classes, jobs, extracurriculars, leadership positions and trying to maintain some semblance of a social life, there are never enough hours in the day. AI makes things easier. [...] I am not asking anyone to abandon AI. I use it, and I recognize the benefits it provides. But I do think we need to become more conscientious about when we use it and what we are asking it to do for us. Let it help with the tedious tasks. Let it serve as a resource. But do not let it become a substitute for your own intellectual development. [...] There is also something to be said about individuality. items.title: AI and your job: Threat or opportunity?
items.summary:
MOBILE, Ala. (WALA) - Artificial intelligence is becoming a bigger part of everyday life, raising questions about what the technology could mean for workers and their jobs.

Some economists believe AI poses a particular threat to entry-level and repetitive work, including call center, data entry and junior copywriting jobs, according to The Wall Street Journal. Those tasks may be easier to automate. [...] But AI could also create opportunities. A Bloomberg article points to potential job growth in construction and manufacturing as companies build data centers and produce the chips that power the technology. Some higher-skilled office workers could also benefit if AI helps them become more productive. [...] The long-term impact on jobs remains unclear, but workers can take steps to prepare. Exploring AI chatbots, writing assistants and other tools may help people find ways to work more efficiently and develop skills that complement the technology.

results.input: Viết giúp mình một hàm Python tính Fibonacci bằng recursion.

result.actual_text:
Dưới đây là hàm Python tính số Fibonacci bằng phương pháp đệ quy (recursion):

### 1. Hàm đệ quy cơ bản

```python
def fibonacci(n):
    # Kiểm tra điều kiện đầu vào
    if n < 0:
        raise ValueError("n phải là số nguyên không âm.")
    
    # Trường hợp cơ sở (Base cases)
    if n == 0:
        return 0
    if n == 1:
        return 1
    
    # Bước đệ quy (Recursive step)
    return fibonacci(n - 1) + fibonacci(n - 2)

# Ví dụ sử dụng:
n = 10
print(f"Số Fibonacci thứ {n} là: {fibonacci(n)}")
# Kết quả: 55
```

---

### 2. Tối ưu hóa đệ quy bằng Memoization (sử dụng `@lru_cache`)

Hàm đệ quy thuần túy có độ phức tạp thời gian là **$O(2^n)$**, dễ bị chậm hoặc tràn bộ nhớ khi $n$ lớn do tính lại các giá trị trùng lặp. Bạn có thể tối ưu thành **$O(n)$** bằng cách dùng `lru_cache`:

```python
from functools import lru_cache

@lru_cache(maxsize=None)
def fibonacci_memo(n):
    if n < 0:
        raise ValueError("n phải là số nguyên không âm.")
    if n == 0:
        return 0
    if n == 1:
        return 1
    return fibonacci_memo(n - 1) + fibonacci_memo(n - 2)

# Ví dụ sử dụng với n lớn
n = 50
print(f"Số Fibonacci thứ {n} là: {fibonacci_memo(n)}")
# Kết quả: 12586269025
```

The first approach requires extensive engineering, while the second needs enormous amounts of data and time. [...] Berkeley-based Ambi Robotics, which specializes in logistics and warehouse order fulfillment, applied the new methods earlier this year to analyze parcel sorting data and test updates to robot behavior. Tests showed an increased capacity of over 15,000 packages sorted annually per robot; the change is now deployed across 30% of the company’s U.S. fleet. [...] Ken Goldberg

“Agentic robotics is a fundamental shift in how robots are controlled,” Goldberg said. “Instead of collecting massive amounts of data and hand-tuning every behavior, teams of agents can quickly generate, test and refine robot programs that allow human engineers to interpret how the programs work for fine-tuning and verification.”

items.title: Weekend hack: HackerTube. I was annoyed with YouTube's recommendations so I had Claude filter down 43M comments over 20
items.summary:
Weekend hack: HackerTube. I was annoyed with YouTube's recommendations so I had Claude filter down 43M comments over 20 years of HN to 6,454 videos that keep being recommended. *Significantly* better viewing experience, ~2 hours with Opus 5.5:
https://t.co/JIhXN7OSh1

- Excellent recs without any logins (state is kept in local browser session)
- Thumbnail is a representative frame from middle of the video instead of the super duper A/B test hyper-optimized user uploads
- Underlying data from the comment analysis as one zip file, point your Claude at it and ask for your own version
- HackerTube Longs ✊

A bit more on the process:
I use Claude Code (desktop app for Mac), Opus 5.5 on Medium effort as my default. I only talk to Claude and have it do everything, the only "manual work" I helped with in tandem was in the browser (reminiscent of MenuGen): 1) I had to create some kind of API key from Google Cloud UI to query YouTube for video metadata, 2) I booted up a VPS box for serving and 3) I bought the domain name. Once the box was up I gave Claude the IP and told it update, secure, harden, deploy and optimize the code, and it did the whole thing.

Many awesome projects that would have normally taken weeks/months even can now be few-shotted for breakfast. What else are we not thinking of.
